cards.q: Which layer delivers data to the right program on a machine, and with what address?
cards.a:
The transport layer, using port numbers

The IP address only gets the packet to the machine; the transport layer (TCP or UDP) uses the destination port to pick the program.

cards.q: What does a router in the middle of the internet look at to forward a packet?
cards.a:
The IP header's destination address

Each layer reads only its own header. A router works at the internet layer and never looks at TCP or application data.

cards.q: With a 1500-byte MTU, how much application data fits in one TCP packet without options?
cards.a:
1460 bytes

1500 minus 20 for the IPv4 header and 20 for the TCP header. 1472 is the figure for UDP, whose header is only 8 bytes.

cards.q: Why do games care so much about header overhead?
cards.a:
Their messages are small and frequent, so headers can outweigh the data

A 40-byte update sent 60 times a second carries more header bytes than data, so game protocols pack data tightly and batch updates.

cards.q: What is the network address of 10.20.30.40/20?
cards.a:
10.20.16.0

The /20 mask is 255.255.240.0: it keeps 10.20 and only the top 4 bits of 30, which is 16. 10.20.30.0 would be the answer for a /24.

cards.q: How many usable hosts does a /26 network have?
cards.a:
62

2^(32-26) = 64 addresses, minus the reserved network and broadcast addresses, gives 62. 126 is the figure for a /25.

cards.q: Why can't an outside computer start a connection to a laptop behind a home router?
cards.a:
NAT only has mappings for connections started from inside

Replies to outgoing connections are translated back using a remembered mapping; an unsolicited packet has no mapping, so the router does not know which device should get it.

2001:db8::1

Leading zeros in each group are dropped and the one run of zero groups becomes `::`. `::` may appear only once in an address.

cards.q: What is the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative server?
cards.a:
The resolver looks names up for clients and caches them; the authoritative server holds a zone's actual records

Your program asks a recursive resolver, which walks the tree if needed and caches what it finds; the records themselves live on each zone's authoritative servers.

cards.q: Which record type holds an IPv6 address?
cards.a:
AAAA

A holds an IPv4 address and AAAA an IPv6 address (type 28 on the wire).

cards.q: How is the name a.bc encoded as DNS labels?
cards.a:
01 'a' 02 'b' 'c' 00

Each label is preceded by its length, there are no dots on the wire, and the name ends with a zero byte.

cards.q: Why should a program use getaddrinfo instead of sending its own DNS queries?
cards.a:
It uses the system's resolver, cache and hosts file, and handles IPv4 and IPv6

The operating system already knows which resolver to ask, caches answers and reads the hosts file; building DNS packets yourself is for writing DNS tools.

cards.q: What are the three packets of the TCP handshake?
cards.a:
SYN, then SYN+ACK, then ACK

The client sends SYN with its starting sequence number, the server answers SYN+ACK with its own, and the client acknowledges that with ACK. FIN is for closing, not opening.

cards.q: What does a TCP acknowledgement number tell the sender?
cards.a:
That every byte before that number has arrived, and which byte is expected next

An acknowledgement of N means "I have every byte up to N; send N next". The free buffer space is the window, a separate field.

cards.q: What is head-of-line blocking?
cards.a:
Data after a lost TCP segment waiting for its retransmission, even if it already arrived

TCP must deliver bytes in order, so one lost segment holds back everything after it until the retransmission arrives, typically a round trip or more later.

cards.q: Why do fast-paced games send state over UDP?
cards.a:
A late resend of an old update would hold back newer ones

UDP makes no delivery promises at all; the gain is that a lost old update never holds back the newer ones that replace it.

cards.q: What does the default gateway do for your computer?
cards.a:
It receives every packet whose destination is not on the local network

The default route (0.0.0.0/0) names the gateway; packets for the local network are sent directly, and everything else goes to it.

cards.q: Routes 172.16.0.0/12 and 172.16.5.0/24 both match 172.16.5.9. Which is used?
cards.a:
172.16.5.0/24, because it has the longer prefix

When several routes match, the most specific one, with the longest prefix, wins; the order of the table does not matter.

cards.q: How does traceroute find the routers along a path?
cards.a:
It sends packets with increasing TTL values; each router that drops one at zero reports back

Each router decrements the TTL; the one that takes it to zero drops the packet and sends an ICMP "time exceeded" message, revealing itself.

cards.q: A protocol needs 4 round trips and the RTT is 80 ms. Roughly how long does it take, however fast the bandwidth?
cards.a:
About 320 ms

Each round trip costs the RTT whatever the bandwidth, so 4 x 80 ms is about 320 ms. Latency, not bandwidth, decides it.

cards.q: Why try every address getaddrinfo returns?
cards.a:
A name can have several addresses, and some may be unreachable from your network

A name often has both an IPv6 and an IPv4 address, or several servers; trying each until one connects copes with the ones you cannot reach.

cards.q: `send` returns 512 when you asked it to send 2000 bytes. What does that mean?
cards.a:
Only 512 bytes were accepted; you must send the remaining 1488 yourself

`send` reports how many bytes went into the socket's buffer, which may be fewer than you asked; the rest is still yours to send.

cards.q: What does `recv` returning 0 mean?
cards.a:
The other side has closed its sending direction: end of stream

0 is end of stream. An error is `SOCKET_ERROR`, and a blocking `recv` waits rather than returning 0 when nothing has arrived.

cards.q: `connect` fails with error 10061. What is the likely cause?
cards.a:
Nothing is listening on that port at that address

10061 is `WSAECONNREFUSED`: the machine answered with a reset because no program listens on that port. A timeout is 10060, and a taken port is 10048.

cards.q: What does `accept` return?
cards.a:
A new socket for the accepted connection, while the listener keeps listening

Each accepted connection gets its own socket; the listening socket stays as it was and carries on accepting.

cards.q: Why does a test that sends one small message over loopback hide framing bugs?
cards.a:
Locally a small message arrives in one `recv`; real networks split it

TCP is a byte stream everywhere; locally a small message just happens to arrive in one piece, so code without a read loop seems to work.

cards.q: Why call `shutdown(s, SD_SEND)` before `closesocket`?
cards.a:
It tells the peer you have finished sending while still letting you receive its remaining data

The FIN lets the peer read everything and reply; closing while its data is unread makes Windows send a reset, and data can be lost.

cards.q: A restarted server fails to `bind` with `WSAEADDRINUSE`. What might be the cause?
cards.a:
Connections from the previous run are still in TIME_WAIT on that port

The side that closed first keeps old connections in TIME_WAIT for a while, which can stop an immediate restart from binding the same port.

cards.q: How is the port 443 (0x01BB) written in network byte order?
cards.a:
01 BB

Network byte order is big-endian: the most significant byte first. BB 01 is how a little-endian x86 machine stores it in memory.

cards.q: What does the first byte 0x46 of an IPv4 header say?
cards.a:
Version 4, header length 6 words (24 bytes), so 4 bytes of options

The high half is the version (4) and the low half the header length in 32-bit words: 6 x 4 = 24 bytes, 4 more than the 20-byte minimum.

cards.q: Which of these is a real reason not to cast a packet buffer to a C++ struct?
cards.a:
The compiler may insert padding between fields, so offsets do not match the wire

Padding, host byte order, implementation-defined bit-field order, misaligned reads and aliasing all break the cast; reading fields one by one avoids them.

cards.q: How do you check an Internet checksum?
cards.a:
Sum every 16-bit word including the checksum with one's complement addition; a correct packet gives 0xFFFF

Including the checksum in the one's complement sum makes a correct packet come out as 0xFFFF before the final NOT, or zero after it.

cards.q: What does `WSAEWOULDBLOCK` from `recv` on a non-blocking socket mean?
cards.a:
No data is available right now; it is not an error

A non-blocking call that cannot do anything yet fails with `WSAEWOULDBLOCK`; try again when `select` or `WSAPoll` says the socket is ready.

cards.q: What does an event loop wait in, and why?
cards.a:
In `select` or `WSAPoll`, which sleep until any socket is ready, so it uses no CPU while idle

Waiting in one call for all sockets avoids busy polling; a blocking `recv` on one socket would stall every other client.

cards.q: Why does each connection need its own output queue in an event loop?
cards.a:
Because `send` may take only part of the data or none, and the rest must wait until the socket is writable

The loop cannot wait in `send`, so unsent bytes are kept per connection and sent when `POLLWRNORM` reports the socket writable again.

cards.q: Why must an event loop never do slow work inline?
cards.a:
While it works, it serves no other connection, so every client waits

One thread serves every connection, so anything slow (a disk read, heavy computation) stalls all of them; push it to worker threads instead.

cards.q: How many datagrams can one `recvfrom` return?
cards.a:
Exactly one, whole

Each `recvfrom` returns exactly one datagram; if the buffer is too small, the rest of that datagram is discarded, not kept for the next call.

cards.q: Why keep UDP payloads under about 1200 bytes?
cards.a:
Larger datagrams may be fragmented, and losing any fragment loses the whole datagram

A datagram over the path's MTU is split at the IP level; one lost piece loses it all, so staying comfortably under the MTU is safer.

cards.q: Which two things must an answer to a UDP request match before it is accepted?
cards.a:
The address and port the request was sent to, and the request's id

Anything else may be a stray packet, a late answer to an earlier attempt, or a forged reply, and is ignored.

cards.q: What does `WSAECONNRESET` on a UDP socket mean on Windows?
cards.a:
An earlier datagram hit a closed port and ICMP reported it

Nothing was listening at the port an earlier datagram went to, so an ICMP port unreachable came back. UDP has no connections; Windows reports the ICMP message on the next `recvfrom`, and a server talking to many clients should ignore it.

cards.q: What ends the headers of an HTTP/1.1 message?
cards.a:
An empty line: `\r\n` on its own

The headers end at the first blank line; the body, if any, follows it. `Content-Length` says how long the body is, not where the headers stop.

cards.q: Why is the `Host` header required in HTTP/1.1?
cards.a:
One server address can host many websites, and `Host` says which one the request is for

The connection already reaches the right machine; `Host` picks the site on it, because one IP often serves many sites.

cards.q: A client receives status 418 and does not know it. How should it treat it?
cards.a:
As a generic 4xx client error, like 400

The first digit gives the class; an unknown 4xx is treated like 400.

cards.q: Why must every response on a persistent connection have a `Content-Length` or a chunked body?
cards.a:
Otherwise the client cannot tell where the response ends and the next one begins

The same connection carries several messages, so each must say where it ends; a response without either can only end by closing the connection.

cards.q: How does a parser know it has received all the headers?
cards.a:
It has found the first `\r\n\r\n` in the stream

The head ends at the empty line. Data arrives in arbitrary chunks, so one `recv` says nothing about message boundaries.

cards.q: A response has `Content-Length: 120` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`. What should a strict parser do?
cards.a:
Reject it as ambiguous

Parsers that resolve this ambiguity differently are what makes request smuggling possible, so a strict parser refuses the message.

cards.q: What sizes do the chunk size lines `4`, `6` and `E` announce?
cards.a:
4, 6 and 14 bytes

Chunk sizes are hexadecimal, and E is 14.

cards.q: A GET request has no `Content-Length` and no `Transfer-Encoding`. How long is its body?
cards.a:
It has no body

Without either header a request has no body. Only a response body may run until the connection closes.

cards.q: Which part of a URL is never sent to the server?
cards.a:
The fragment, after `#`

The browser keeps the fragment to jump within a page. The path and query go in the request line, the host and port in the `Host` header.

cards.q: How is the character é percent-encoded?
cards.a:
`%C3%A9`, its UTF-8 bytes

Each byte of the character's UTF-8 encoding is written as `%` and two hex digits; é is the two bytes C3 A9.

cards.q: Why decode each part of a URL only after splitting it at its separators?
cards.a:
An encoded separator such as `%2F` is data; decoding first would turn it into a real separator

`%2F` inside a name must stay part of that name; decoding before splitting would create a new path segment.

cards.q: In form encoding, how are a space and a plus sign written?
cards.a:
A space as `+`, and a plus sign as `%2B`

Form encoding writes a space as `+`, so a real `+` must be encoded. When parsing, turn `+` into a space before percent-decoding.

cards.q: A path matches a route but the method does not. What status should the server send?
cards.a:
405 Method Not Allowed

The resource exists, so 404 would mislead; 405 with `Allow` tells the client which methods would work.

cards.q: Why should a server send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`?
cards.a:
So browsers use the declared `Content-Type` instead of guessing

A browser guessing the type could treat uploaded data as script or HTML; `nosniff` makes it trust the server's type.

cards.q: Why reject a `..` that climbs above the root instead of clamping it?
cards.a:
It is never a legitimate request, and rejecting avoids subtle mistakes in clamping

A real link never climbs above the root, so such a request is an attack; refusing it is simpler and safer than trying to repair it.

cards.q: Which of these must a Windows file server reject in a request path?
cards.a:
A `:` (drive letters and alternate data streams)

Backslashes, colons, device names such as `CON` or `NUL`, and names ending in a dot or space all mean something special to Windows.

cards.q: What three guarantees does TLS add to a connection?
cards.a:
Confidentiality, integrity and authentication of the server

Reliability and ordering already come from TCP; TLS encrypts, detects tampering and proves who the server is.

cards.q: Does `*.justloofy.dev` match `a.b.justloofy.dev`?
cards.a:
No: a wildcard matches exactly one label

The wildcard stands for exactly one whole label, so it matches `xenon.justloofy.dev` but neither `a.b.justloofy.dev` nor `justloofy.dev`.

cards.q: Why does the ClientHello carry the hostname (SNI)?
cards.a:
One address hosts many sites; the certificate is chosen before HTTP

The `Host` header is only sent inside the encrypted channel, too late to choose the certificate, so the name goes in the ClientHello.

cards.q: Why is turning off certificate verification never an acceptable fix?
cards.a:
Anyone can then pretend to be the server and read your data

Encryption still happens, but with whoever answered; without authentication an attacker in the middle can read and change everything.

cards.q: What is the difference between a capture filter and a display filter?
cards.a:
A capture filter decides what is recorded; a display filter only hides packets and can be changed afterwards

Packets a capture filter drops are gone for good, so capture broadly and narrow the view with display filters.

cards.q: A pcap file's magic number reads as `0xD4C3B2A1`. What does that mean?
cards.a:
The file was written in the other byte order, so every field must be read big-endian

The magic number doubles as a byte-order mark. The nanosecond variant is `0xA1B23C4D`, a different value.

cards.q: Why can a packet's captured length be smaller than its original length?
cards.a:
The capture stored at most the snapshot length of each packet

A packet longer than the snapshot length is truncated in the file; decoders must cope with that.

cards.q: What must you enable to capture traffic to 127.0.0.1 on Windows?
cards.a:
Npcap's loopback capture support

Loopback traffic never touches a real network card, so it needs Npcap's loopback adapter.

cards.q: An Ethernet frame's bytes 12-13 are `86 DD`. What comes next?
cards.a:
An IPv6 header

EtherType `0x86DD` is IPv6; IPv4 is `0x0800`, ARP `0x0806` and a VLAN tag `0x8100`.

cards.q: The first byte of an IPv4 header is `0x47`. Where does the TCP header start?
cards.a:
28 bytes into the IP header

The low nibble is IHL, the header length in 32-bit words: 7 x 4 = 28 bytes, so 8 bytes of options follow the fixed 20.

cards.q: Why use the IPv4 total length instead of the frame's length to find the end of the data?
cards.a:
Short frames are padded, and the padding is not IP data

Ethernet pads small frames to 60 bytes; only the total length says where the IP packet really ends.

cards.q: Which IPv4 fragments carry the TCP header?
cards.a:
Only the first one, with fragment offset 0

The later fragments carry continuation data; a decoder that reads a TCP header from them reads garbage.

cards.q: A TCP flags byte is `0x12`. Which flags are set?
cards.a:
SYN and ACK

0x12 = 0x10 (ACK) + 0x02 (SYN): the second packet of the handshake.

cards.q: The data offset nibble is 8. Where does the payload start?
cards.a:
32 bytes into the TCP header

The data offset counts 32-bit words: 8 x 4 = 32 bytes, so 12 bytes of options follow the fixed 20.

cards.q: Why does a SYN with no data still use a sequence number?
cards.a:
SYN and FIN each count as one byte of sequence space, so they can be acknowledged

That is why the handshake acknowledges "seq + 1". Data segments use one number per byte, and pure ACKs use none.

cards.q: Why do captures on the sending machine often show bad TCP checksums?
cards.a:
The network card fills in the checksum after the capture point

With checksum offloading the card computes it in hardware, so the captured copy still has a blank or partial checksum.

cards.q: How do you put both directions of one connection under the same key?
cards.a:
Order the two endpoints canonically, for example the lower address and port first

Replies have the four-tuple reversed; sorting the two endpoints gives both directions the same key.

cards.q: A server's SYN-ACK has relative ack 1. What does it acknowledge?
cards.a:
The client's SYN, which used relative sequence number 0

The SYN takes up one sequence number, so acknowledging it means "I expect byte 1 next".

cards.q: How does a retransmission appear in a capture?
cards.a:
As a segment whose bytes were already sent earlier

The sender resends the same bytes, so the range repeats. Repeated acknowledgements are duplicate ACKs, which often trigger a retransmission but are not one.

cards.q: A SYN is answered immediately by a RST. What happened?
cards.a:
Connection refused: nothing was listening on that port

A RST in reply to a SYN means no program listens on that port; an orderly close uses FIN in both directions.

cards.q: In a DNS header, how do you tell a query from a response?
cards.a:
By the top bit of the flags, QR: 0 for a query, 1 for a response

A response can have zero answers (for example "no such name"), so only the QR bit is reliable.

cards.q: What does a TLS record with content type 23 contain?
cards.a:
Encrypted application data

Type 22 is handshake, 21 alert and 23 application data, which a capture cannot read.

cards.q: Where in a capture can you see which website an HTTPS connection was for?
cards.a:
In the server name indication extension (type 0) of the ClientHello

The `Host` header is encrypted; the SNI in the ClientHello is sent in clear text, unless Encrypted Client Hello is used.

cards.q: Why must a decoder check every length field against the bytes available?
cards.a:
Captured data can be truncated or malformed, and trusting a length would read past the end

Snapshot limits, split segments and hostile input all produce lengths that do not fit; a robust decoder reports "truncated" instead.

cards.q: What is head-of-line blocking?
cards.a:
One lost segment holding back later data that already arrived

The later data is in the receive buffer but unusable until the gap is filled. Combining small writes is Nagle's algorithm, a different source of delay.

cards.q: Why is resending an old player position pointless?
cards.a:
Newer positions have been sent since, and only the latest state matters

By the time an old position could be resent, several newer ones exist; that is why such data is sent unreliably, newest-wins.

cards.q: How does a UDP "connection" in a game protocol end?
cards.a:
By timing out after hearing nothing for a few seconds

UDP has no FIN; both sides send at a steady rate, so silence for a few seconds is how a connection is known to be gone.

cards.q: Why make the network simulator deterministic?
cards.a:
So a failing test loses the same packets every time and can be debugged

With a fixed pattern or seeded generator, a failure can be repeated exactly; random losses that change every run make bugs vanish when you look for them.

cards.q: Why does `a > b` fail for sequence numbers?
cards.a:
After the counter wraps, a newer packet has a smaller number than an older one

A 16-bit counter wraps from 65 535 to 0, so packet 2 is newer than 65 534; half-range comparison handles that.

cards.q: What is `sequenceDifference(1, 65535)`?
cards.a:
2

Subtracting in 16-bit unsigned arithmetic gives 2, and as a signed 16-bit value that is still 2: packet 1 is two newer, across the wrap.

cards.q: A packet arrives whose number is 500 behind the latest, with a 256-number window. What happens?
cards.a:
It is dropped: it is too old to tell whether it is a duplicate

The receiver only remembers the last 256 numbers, so it cannot tell whether a packet older than that was already seen.

cards.q: Why might a game drop a late position update but still read the chat message in the same packet?
cards.a:
Positions are newest-wins, so old ones are useless, but each chat message must be delivered

Whether old data is useful depends on the kind of data, not on the packet, so the decision is made per kind.

cards.q: With `ack = 200` and only bit 0 of `ackBits` set, which packets were received?
cards.a:
200 and 199

Bit *i* stands for packet `ack - 1 - i`, so bit 0 is 199; `ack` itself, 200, is always received.

cards.q: Why put acknowledgements in every packet instead of sending separate ack packets?
cards.a:
Both sides send constantly, so acks ride along for a few bytes

Piggybacked acks cost only a few header bytes, and since every packet repeats the last 33, losing some of them does no harm: any one that arrives tells the whole story.

cards.q: The latest is 50 and packet 90 arrives. What happens to the bits?
cards.a:
They all become 0, since a jump of 40 is more than 32 bits

Every old bit falls off, including the one for 50, which would be bit 39, beyond the 32-bit field. Shifting a 32-bit value by 32 or more is undefined, so this case is handled separately.

cards.q: Why must the sender remember which packets were already acknowledged?
cards.a:
Each packet is acked many times but is delivered only once

Every incoming packet repeats the last 33 acks; without remembering, the same delivery would be counted again and again.

cards.q: The first RTT sample is 80 ms. What are srtt, rttvar and the timeout?
cards.a:
srtt 80 ms, rttvar 40 ms, timeout 240 ms

The first sample sets srtt = R and rttvar = R / 2, so rto = 80 + 4 x 40 = 240 ms before clamping.

cards.q: Why add 4 × rttvar to the timeout rather than using srtt alone?
cards.a:
So a normal but slower-than-average round trip is not treated as a loss

Half of all round trips are slower than the average; a margin based on the variation stops them triggering needless resends.

cards.q: What does Karn's rule say?
cards.a:
Do not take an RTT sample from anything that was retransmitted

After a resend you cannot tell whether the ack is for the first copy or the second, so the sample would be wrong. Doubling the timeout is backoff, a separate rule.

cards.q: A receiver expecting message 10 receives 12, then 10. What is delivered and when?
cards.a:
Nothing at 12 (it is buffered); at 10, message 10 is delivered, and 12 waits for 11

Ordered delivery hands over the next expected id plus any buffered ones that follow it; 12 does not follow 10, so it waits.

cards.q: Why not let IP fragment large UDP datagrams?
cards.a:
Losing any one fragment loses the whole datagram

Fragmentation multiplies the loss rate; some networks also drop fragments, and IPv6 routers do not fragment at all. So games keep datagrams under about 1200 bytes and split data themselves.

cards.q: A fragment says index 7, count 5. What should the receiver do?
cards.a:
Drop it: the index must be below the count

A value out of range is a dropped packet, never an out-of-range write; indexes run from 0 to count - 1.

cards.q: Why do incomplete blocks need a timeout?
cards.a:
A lost fragment, or a malicious sender, would otherwise keep reassembly buffers in memory forever

Without timeouts and a limit on blocks in progress, memory can be used up by blocks that will never complete.

cards.q: What does a priority accumulator guarantee that plain priorities do not?
cards.a:
That low-priority objects are still sent eventually

Each tick adds an object's priority to its score and sending resets it, so far-away objects update less often but are never starved.

cards.q: Why do clients send inputs rather than positions?
cards.a:
So a client cannot simply claim where it is or what it hit

With an authoritative server, clients only say what they want to do; the server's simulation decides what actually happened, which is the basis of fair play.

cards.q: A client sends a movement vector of length 3. What should the server do?
cards.a:
Clamp it to the allowed maximum (length 1)

Input values are never trusted as they arrive; anything beyond what the rules allow is clamped or rejected.

cards.q: Why cap the number of ticks run in one frame?
cards.a:
To avoid a spiral where catching up takes so long that the next frame falls even further behind

After a long pause, running hundreds of catch-up ticks makes each frame slower still; capping them and dropping the backlog breaks the spiral.

cards.q: What does `alpha` in the accumulator loop represent?
cards.a:
How far the time is between the last tick and the next

`alpha = accumulator / step` is a fraction from 0 to 1, letting a 144 Hz screen draw smoothly between two 60 Hz simulation states.

cards.q: A map is 0 to 4 096 units wide and positions use 16 bits. What is the step size?
cards.a:
About 0.06 units

4 096 / 65 535 is roughly 0.0625 units. 0.015 is the step for a 1 000-unit map.

cards.q: Why should the server simulate with quantised values?
cards.a:
So the client's rebuilt state matches the server's exactly

If the server kept full precision, the client's dequantised values would differ slightly from the truth, and the two would disagree.

cards.q: Why encode against the last acknowledged snapshot rather than the last one sent?
cards.a:
The last one sent might have been lost, while the acknowledged one is known to be on the client

Applying changes to a baseline the client does not have would leave its world silently wrong; an acknowledged baseline is safe under loss.

cards.q: What does an entity look like in a delta if it has not changed?
cards.a:
It is not included at all

Unchanged entities are left out entirely; new ones have every bit set and removed ones get a marker.

cards.q: Why render other players in the past?
cards.a:
So the client already has snapshots on both sides of the render time and can blend smoothly

Rendering about two snapshot intervals behind means the snapshot after the render time has usually arrived, hiding jitter and the odd lost snapshot.

cards.q: With snapshots at 20 per second, what delay is typical?
cards.a:
About 100 ms, two snapshot intervals

Two intervals cover the gap between snapshots plus some jitter, so one lost snapshot is blended across without anyone noticing.

cards.q: Why use the server's tick numbers instead of arrival times?
cards.a:
Arrival times include jitter; ticks are the states' real times

Interpolation exists to hide jitter; timing snapshots by their arrival would put the jitter straight back.

cards.q: Why limit extrapolation?
cards.a:
Guesses go wrong fast and snap back when real data arrives

A short extrapolation hides a small gap; a long one shows players running into walls and snapping back, so it is capped at about one interval.

cards.q: What does the server need to include for reconciliation to work?
cards.a:
Its state and the number of the last input it applied

Knowing which inputs are already in the state tells the client which pending inputs to drop and which to replay.

cards.q: Why replay pending inputs instead of just jumping to the server's position?
cards.a:
The server's state is a round trip old; replaying catches it up

Without the replay the player would snap back a round trip in time every snapshot, undoing the inputs still on their way.

cards.q: Prediction was perfect. What does reconciliation change on screen?
cards.a:
Nothing: the replay arrives at the same position

Resetting to the confirmed state and replaying the pending inputs gives exactly what was predicted, so there is no visible correction.

cards.q: Why should the client not predict whether its shot killed someone?
cards.a:
Hits decide the game and depend on other players' true positions, so the server must decide them

Only your own movement and animation are predicted; anything that decides the game waits for the server.

cards.q: Why would a perfectly aimed shot miss without lag compensation?
cards.a:
The shooter sees the past, and the target has moved since

Interpolation shows others about 100 ms behind, plus the input's travel time; without rewinding, players would have to aim ahead by their ping.

cards.q: What does the server need to store to rewind?
cards.a:
A short history of each player's position (hitbox) per tick

It rewinds the other players to the tick the shooter saw, interpolating between recorded ticks, and tests the shot there.

cards.q: A client claims it was seeing tick 1 000 while the server is at tick 5 000 and allows 32 ticks of rewind. Which tick is used?
cards.a:
4 968, the oldest allowed

The rewind is clamped to the maximum: 5 000 - 32 = 4 968. A client cannot rewrite history further back than that.

cards.q: Who gets the advantage of lag compensation, and what does the other side experience?
cards.a:
The shooter; the target can be hit after reaching cover on their own screen

Testing against what the shooter saw favours the shooter, causing the "shot around the corner" effect, which is why the rewind is capped.
